English: Introduction to cyber hygiene
What is it?

Cyber hygiene is the set of small, regular habits that keep your phone, accounts, money and personal data safe — just as washing hands keeps germs away. It is not a one-time setting; it is a routine. Most frauds in India do not “hack” a system. They trick a person into giving away an OTP, a PIN, a password or access to a phone. Good habits close those doors before anyone knocks.

Key term            Figure 1.3 · Six everyday risks that cyber hygiene protects against Cyber hygiene           Meaning Social engineering      Simple, regular habits that protect devices, accounts and personal data Phishing                Tricking people with urgency, fear or greed instead of breaking technology A fake message, call or website that pretends to be trusted in order to steal details

A shopping site Ravi once used was breached. Criminals tried his leaked email and password on Instagram and Gmail — they worked, because he used the same password everywhere. Within an hour his friends received “urgent” requests for money from his account. Lesson: one reused password turned one leak into three takeovers. Unique passphrases and two-step verification would have stopped it.
Ask yourself
Am I careful when clicking links, downloading files or sharing information online?
Do I use the same password for more than one important account?
Is two-step verification on for my WhatsApp, email and banking apps?
Stop interacting with anything suspicious: do not reply, click or forward.
Screenshot the message, number, link and time before deleting anything.
Suspicious call or SMS: Chakshu on sancharsaathi.gov.in. Money lost: 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in.
Your OTP, UPI PIN, CVV, password and WhatsApp code are keys, not information. No bank, police officer or company will ever ask for them.
Password and account security
What is it?

A weak password is short or personal (a name, a birth year, 12345678). A strong one is long, random and used for only one account. A passphrase of four random words is both strong and easy to remember. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second check after the password: a code from an app, a prompt on your phone, a passkey or a fingerprint. Even if a password leaks, the account stays locked.

Device security and app permissions
What is it?

Your phone holds bank apps, photos, contacts and OTPs. Device security rests on four building blocks: a screen lock, updates, apps from trusted sources only, and minimum permissions. A permission is an app's request to use the camera, microphone, contacts, location, SMS or files. Give each app only what it needs to do its job. An app installed from a link (an APK file) can read OTPs and mirror your screen.

Privacy and personal information
What is it?

Personal information identifies you (name, phone, address, date of birth, photos). Sensitive information can cause serious harm if misused (Aadhaar, PAN, bank details, health records). Your digital footprint is everything about you online — what you post, what others post and what apps collect. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, you have the right to know how your data is used, to correct it, to ask for its erasure and to complain to the organisation and then the Data Protection Board.

Neha posted a week-long holiday with live location while her house in Pune stood empty. A neighbour's CCTV later showed strangers checking the door. Lesson: share trips after you return, switch off live location on posts, and keep the account private.
Your digital footprint can stay online for years. Think before you share, and share sensitive documents only in masked form and only for a verified need.
Safe internet practices
What is it?

Safe internet use is about where you connect, what you click and what you keep a copy of. A fake website looks exactly like the real one; the difference is in the address and in how you arrived there.

Priya logged in to her email on a cybercafé computer and left without logging out. The next user reset her social media passwords through her inbox. Lesson: private window, no saved passwords, log out, close the browser — every time.

Did I check the full website address before entering details?
Do I have a backup of my important files?
Entered details on a suspicious page? Stop and change that password from a safe device.

Inform the bank if card or UPI details were shared; report on cybercrime.gov.in.
Always verify before connecting, clicking, downloading or sharing information online.
Basic cyber incident response
Responder
What is it?

A cyber incident is any event that harms or may harm someone's accounts, devices, money or safety. A guides the person to the right channel. You do not investigate the criminal, promise that money will come back, ask for the person's password or OTP, or take their phone without consent.

Role limits

A First Responder identifies, stabilises, preserves and routes. Complex or high-risk cases go to the police, the bank, CERT-In (for organisations) or other authorised professionals. This is covered in depth in Modules 4 to 6.
